title: adaptive-ephemeral-pools-and-fidelity-fencing-proposal
content:
Context
We need a practical design that lets Dedicated customers keep predictable baseline performance while allowing controlled, low-latency bursts. Existing reserved capacity models are too static (commit -> idle capacity) or too aggressive in evicting during demand spikes. This proposal combines two ideas: short-lived "ephemeral warm pools" that can be prewarmed per-tenant and a lightweight "fidelity fencing" policy that dynamically trades inference fidelity (quantization / precision / model variant) to expand burst capacity without violating latency SLOs for higher-tier tenants.

Problem statement
- Customers want predictable baseline throughput + occasional fast bursts for traffic spikes (marketing launches, events).
- Current approaches: big reserved buffers (costly) or sloppy overcommit (noisy neighbor risk).
- We need an autoscaler that: 1) minimizes cold-start latency for bursts, 2) enforces tenant isolation so one tenant's burst cannot degrade others beyond a bounded tolerance, 3) exposes clear economics (credits / spend) and policy knobs.

Goals
- Provide sub-second warm-starts for common generator models in 95% of burst events.
- Limit cross-tenant latency degradation to <5% of baseline p95 for tenants in same pool during a controlled burst.
- Enable tenants to define fidelity policies that allow temporary model-variant fallbacks during sustained overloads (e.g., quantized variant or smaller model family).
- Make bursting visible in cost/metering and add a credit-based billing mechanism so customers understand tradeoffs.

Non-goals
- This doc does not propose new billing contracts; it suggests a credit ledger model for design only.
- We are not designing hardware-level preemption in detail (left to infra).

User stories
- As a platform owner I want each tenant to have a small ephemeral warm pool that can be used for microbursts without cold starts.
- As a tenant admin I want to set a fidelity policy that lets the platform automatically downgrade to a quantized variant when capacity is tight.
- As an SRE I want automatic noisy-neighbor detection and soft-eviction that respects taint markers and tenant priorities.
- As a billing owner I want the system to charge burst credit usage separately so customers see the marginal cost of bursts.

Design overview (high-level)
1) Ephemeral warm pools (EWP): per-tenant small pool of prewarmed workers kept at low idle for a rolling window (configurable: 0-10 workers depending on customer tier). Pools are "ephemeral" — they can be created quickly and reclaimed. EWPs are cheaper than full reserved slots because they share memory and can reuse quantized kernels.

2) Concurrency credit ledger: Tenants earn credits from reserved capacity (monthly commitment converts to baseline credits) and can purchase additional burst credits. Credits are spent when ephemeral pool is used beyond baseline or when fallback fidelity policies are triggered. Ledger is time-windowed (daily bucket) and supports overdraft behavior with configurable penalties.

3) Fidelity fencing: Each tenant sets an ordered list of allowed model variants (e.g., rwd-32b-fp16, rwd-32b-int8, rwd-7b-fp16) plus conditions (latency threshold, cost cap). Under soft overload, the runtime can switch requests to the next variant on the list for that tenant. Fallbacks respect semantic constraints (function calls, streaming) and are annotated in response metadata.

4) Isolation controls: Soft fences, hard fences, and tenancy priorities. Soft fences allow limited resource sharing with graceful degradation; hard fences block eviction entirely (enterprise tier only). The orchestrator enforces per-tenant token budgets, concurrent-request caps, and isolation weights in the scheduler.

Autoscaling behavior
- Fast path: if request fits within EWP concurrency, dispatch immediately.
- If not, try to borrow from cross-tenant ephemeral pool buffer (bounded per-pool) if tenant has credits and is allowed by isolation policy.
- If still exceeding, consult fidelity policy to downgrade to an allowed variant. Downgrade is also gated by a per-tenant "fidelity-hedge" rate (avoid mass simultaneous downgrades).
- Fallback: if downgrade not possible and credits exhausted, either queue with a bounded wait or return a 503 with structured retry info (Retry-After and suggested variant).

Credit model details (sketch)
- Baseline credits: 1 credit = 1 worker-second of ephemeral use at baseline fidelity. Monthly committed capacity auto-converts to weekly/daily credits.
- Burst credits: purchased or borrowed from shared marketplace. Borrowing allows temporary overdraft flagged in billing.
- Taking from credits should be visible in console and in trace headers for debugging.

Latency and fairness guarantees
- Isolation weight algorithm: scheduler computes per-tenant weight = reserved_capacity * priority_factor + ephemeral_credits * short_term_weight. During contention, the scheduler enforces max fair-share delta so that no tenant's p95 increases beyond configured percent.
- Goal: default max degradation = 5% p95 for tenants in same reliability class. Can be tightened per-tenant with hard-fence.

Operational considerations and runbook (outline)
- Metrics to surface: EWP fill ratio, credit-burn rate, p95 per-tenant, eviction_count, fidelity-fallback-events, inter-tenant-latency-delta.
- Alerts: fidelity-fallback-rate > 1% sustained for 10m, credit-overdraft > threshold, EWP-misfires > 2% (fail to prewarm).
- Runbook snippets: 
  - If fidelity-fallback spikes: check model variant health, kernel failures, and recent deploys. Roll back recent runtime changes if correlated.
  - If unfair latency observed: simulate with historical trace, compute scheduler weights, and trigger emergency soft-quota to offending tenant.

Safety and guardrails
- No automatic downgrade for requests flagged with must-preserve-fidelity (tenant header).
- Rate limit number of simultaneous downgrades to avoid sudden quality cliffs.
- All fidelity downgrades and credit usages are logged and surfaced to tenant via API metadata.

Simulation & rollout plan
1) Simulation: run two-week historical trace through emulator to compute expected EWP sizes and credit burn for top 200 tenants.
2) Canary: enable EWPs for 5% of tenants (non-critical), monitor fallback rates and inter-tenant latency deltas for 2 weeks.
3) Phased rollout: gradually increase to 25%/50% with expanded guardrails and ops playbook.

Acceptance metrics
- Cold-start probability during burst < 10% (measured across canary tenants).
- Average credit burn for median tenant < predicted budget (simulation).
- No tenant experiences >5% p95 increase attributable to other tenants during canary.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- Billing model integration: should credit overdrafts be billed at premium or cause soft-throttle? (ops vs sales decision)
- How to represent fidelity downgrades in SLAs and legal docs? (requires legal review)
- Quantization compatibility: some model features (safety classifiers, tool-calling) may not tolerate lower fidelity; how to encode those constraints in policies?

Next steps / immediate action items
- Build load simulator job using last 3 months of production traces (owner: infra simulation team).
- Prototype a minimal ephemeral worker pool implementation and trace header for credit accounting (owner: serving-runtime).
- Product: finalize fidelity policy UI/CLI and decide on default policy for free-tier vs enterprise-tier.
- Legal/billing: propose billing semantics for credit overdraft and present to pricing council.

Notes to reviewers
- This is a feature-focused PRD sketch; design assumes existing scheduler primitives for weights and preemption. We intentionally defer low-level kernel/quantization engineering decisions to infra/research.
- Looking for feedback on: credit unit math, default EWP sizing by tenant profile, and acceptable default degradation bounds.

TODOs
- Add example API payloads for specifying fidelity policies and for retrieving credit balance.
- Wireframe console views for credit ledger and fidelity activity timeline.
- Run initial cost model with finance to estimate unit economics per credit.
